name: Avatar
reviewNotes: Manual readthrough: safe as a small identity surface only if fallback initials, alt text, and crop behavior are explicit.
Do not use it as decoration when the real task is user identification or trust signaling.

specificPushback: Avatar looks low-risk, but that still does not make it a default choice; verify semantics, fallback content, and the surrounding flow before promoting it.

killSwitch: Any flow where missing image removes user identification clarity.
manualDecision.whyNow: Identity cues are useful but frequently misused as decorative noise.
mustProve: Fallback initials and alt semantics are always present.
Avatar does not replace explicit identity labels in critical contexts.

name: badge
reviewNotes: Manual readthrough: this is a label-adjacent utility, not a substitute for explanatory text.
Use it for status, category, or tiny counts; do not let it carry meaning that the copy should actually say.

specificPushback: Badge is too small to carry real meaning on its own; if the label matters, say it in text instead of relying on the visual chip.

killSwitch: Any use where chip color is the sole carrier of critical meaning.
manualDecision.whyNow: Badge density is high value only when status vocabulary is controlled.
mustProve: Badge vocabulary is finite and documented.
Critical meaning is duplicated in visible text, not chip color only.

name: CommandPalette
reviewNotes: Manual readthrough: only worth it if the product actually has command discovery, not just because it feels advanced.
The feature is high leverage but easy to overbuild; keep the command set small and obvious.

specificPushback: CommandPalette is easy to overstate: if users cannot predict commands or recall them from memory, the surface becomes a novelty layer instead of a productivity tool.

killSwitch: Search index drift creates stale or misleading command results.
manualDecision.whyNow: High leverage surface that can become performative complexity if command grammar is weak.
mustProve: Top tasks can be completed faster than via visible nav.
Keyboard and screen-reader flows are validated in production-like data.

name: CommandMenu
reviewNotes: Manual readthrough: good for compact action surfaces, but only when the menu model is genuinely discoverable.
If it becomes the only way to reach a command, that is a product navigation smell, not a feature.

specificPushback: CommandMenu should not be the primary way to hide essential actions; if users need it to find core features, the information architecture is already too thin.

killSwitch: Users require command menu to find core product actions.
manualDecision.whyNow: Useful for dense action sets but dangerous when it hides primary actions.
mustProve: Essential actions still exist in visible IA.
Action labels remain unambiguous under localization.

name: ConfirmDialog
reviewNotes: Manual readthrough: this is a high-risk surface because it can turn a destructive action into a mistaken click.
The copy, focus order, and default button bias matter more than the chrome.

specificPushback: ConfirmDialog is a legal-and-product-risk surface, not a reusable convenience component; if the message is vague, the component is wrong by default.

killSwitch: Default focus lands on destructive action or copy is generic.
manualDecision.whyNow: Destructive confirmation flows carry legal, trust, and support risk.
mustProve: Button hierarchy prevents accidental destructive confirmation.
Dialog copy names the irreversible consequence explicitly.

name: CookieConsent
reviewNotes: Manual readthrough: this is compliance-sensitive; treat it as policy UI, not marketing UI.
Never hide the reject path or make acceptance the only obvious action.

specificPushback: CookieConsent is only acceptable when refusal is as visible and usable as acceptance; otherwise the component is doing policy theater.

killSwitch: Reject or customize controls become less visible than accept.
manualDecision.whyNow: Consent mechanics are compliance-critical and cannot be dark-patterned.
mustProve: Reject path parity with accept path is maintained.
Consent state changes are auditable by policy logs.

name: DataTable
reviewNotes: Manual readthrough: strong for operational browsing, weak for storytelling.
Tables fail when sorting, filtering, and empty states are not treated as first-class behavior.

specificPushback: DataTable is a trap if you use it for anything that requires narrative explanation; the component will happily hide the actual decision behind density.

killSwitch: Table is used where narrative explanation is required but absent.
manualDecision.whyNow: Operationally strong but frequently abused for narrative decisions.
mustProve: Sorting/filtering/empty/error states are fully specified.
Key decision outcomes are not hidden in dense tabular noise.

name: AdvancedAutocomplete
reviewNotes: Manual readthrough: useful, but only when keyboard handling, async loading, and empty-state behavior are already solid.
If you need to explain it in the component name, the control may be too clever.

specificPushback: AdvancedAutocomplete can hide complexity behind a pleasant surface, which is exactly why it should not be the first option unless the interaction cost is justified.

killSwitch: Autocomplete suggestions create silent wrong selections.
manualDecision.whyNow: Excellent in constrained vocabularies; harmful when source quality is weak.
mustProve: Keyboard and async loading states are deterministic.
No-results and ambiguity states are explicit and recoverable.

name: DateRangePicker
reviewNotes: Manual readthrough: calendaring controls are notorious for edge cases, especially on mobile and with keyboard users.
Do not ship it without clear min/max constraints and an unambiguous reset path.

specificPushback: DateRangePicker should not be treated as a convenience component; it is a stateful control that can create a lot of user error if the range model is unclear.

killSwitch: Users can submit invalid or ambiguous date ranges.
manualDecision.whyNow: Date logic errors produce silent analytics and workflow corruption.
mustProve: Timezone, locale, and boundary behavior is documented and tested.
Range reset and invalid range behavior is explicit.

name: FileUpload
reviewNotes: Manual readthrough: this is only safe when accepted file types, errors, and retry behavior are explicit.
If the upload flow is ambiguous, the component will expose it immediately.

specificPushback: FileUpload is not a generic drop zone; without exact validation and visible failure states, it becomes a support burden quickly.

killSwitch: Upload accepts disallowed files or hides validation failures.
manualDecision.whyNow: Upload failures are expensive and user-hostile without clear contracts.
mustProve: Accepted types and size constraints are enforced and visible.
Failure and retry paths are observable and actionable.

name: Modal
reviewNotes: Manual readthrough: modals are overused; they should interrupt only when the task really needs blocking attention.
The focus trap and close semantics are not optional details.

specificPushback: Modal should be the exception, not the default; if the user can complete the task inline, the modal is adding friction instead of value.

killSwitch: Modal is used for non-critical content that can be inline.
manualDecision.whyNow: Blocking interaction is often used lazily and damages flow quality.
mustProve: Focus trap, escape, and close semantics are robust.
Inline alternative was considered and rejected with reason.

name: SearchFilter
reviewNotes: Manual readthrough: search filters should feel mechanical and predictable, not clever.
The weakest implementation is the one that looks elegant but hides filter state or resets too easily.

specificPushback: SearchFilter is acceptable only if the active constraints are visible and reversible; otherwise users cannot trust what they are searching.

killSwitch: Hidden filters alter results without visible state.
manualDecision.whyNow: Filtering quality directly affects trust in results.
mustProve: Active filter state is always visible and reversible.
Reset behavior is explicit and non-destructive.

name: Stepper
reviewNotes: Manual readthrough: stepper works when the path is truly sequential; if steps are optional or revisitable, the design starts lying.
It should clarify progress, not create a fake sense of certainty.

specificPushback: Stepper only works when the process is genuinely stepwise; if users can jump around freely, the control becomes misleading decoration.

killSwitch: Stepper implies linearity where process is not linear.
manualDecision.whyNow: Sequential framing helps only when process order is actually real.
mustProve: Step order matches actual workflow constraints.
Users can recover cleanly from prior-step edits.

name: Toast
reviewNotes: Manual readthrough: toasts are for ephemeral, non-blocking status only.
Do not use them for destructive confirmations, compliance, or anything that requires the user to stop and decide.

specificPushback: Toast is a poor container for serious information; if the user must remember it, react to it, or decide from it, use something stronger.

killSwitch: Irreversible decisions are communicated only via toast.
manualDecision.whyNow: Great for ephemeral feedback, unsafe for required decisions.
mustProve: Critical actions never rely solely on toast visibility.
Auto-dismiss timing does not hide actionable information.
